title: Brain Effective Connectivity Estimation via Fourier Spatiotemporal Attention

problem.claim: Estimating brain effective connectivity from fMRI data can support understanding neural mechanisms and disease diagnosis.

gap.claim: Existing spatiotemporal attention methods separately process temporal and spatial attention, overlook inherent spatiotemporal correlations, and are limited by fMRI noise.

contributions.claim: FSTA-EC combines Fourier attention with spatiotemporal attention to capture inter-series spatial dynamics and intra-series temporal dependencies from high-noise fMRI data.
The method converts noisy fMRI data to the frequency domain, maps denoised data back to the physical domain, and simultaneously learns spatiotemporal dynamics.
The authors prove that learnable filters incorporated into fast Fourier transform and inverse fast Fourier transform processes are mathematically equivalent to cyclic convolution.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe FSTA-EC as a novel brain effective connectivity estimation method.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on simulated and real resting-state fMRI datasets are reported to show superior performance against state-of-the-art methods.
Code is reported as available in a public GitHub repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: Brain effective connectivity estimation from fMRI is presented as useful for understanding neural mechanisms and disease diagnosis.
Existing attention modules separate spatial and temporal processing, miss spatiotemporal correlations, and are constrained by noise.
FSTA-EC combines Fourier and spatiotemporal attention to denoise fMRI data and model spatial and temporal dependencies.
The authors provide proofs connecting learnable Fourier-domain filtering with cyclic convolution.
Experiments are reported on simulated and real resting-state fMRI datasets, with code availability stated.

source_observation.claim: The method jointly models spatial and temporal dynamics while applying Fourier-domain processing to high-noise fMRI data.

interpretation.claim: Jointly addressing correlated dimensions and noise may be useful when separate processing loses cross-dimensional structure.

application.claim: For noisy multivariate time-series tasks, consider architectures that combine denoising with joint cross-series and within-series dependency modeling.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this design generalizes beyond fMRI or other similarly structured noisy time series.

unknowns: Specific simulated and real datasets are not identified.
Evaluation metrics, baseline methods, and quantitative performance results are not provided.
The proof details and assumptions behind the cyclic-convolution equivalence are not provided.
Noise characteristics, preprocessing procedures, and limitations are not described.
